detail: wide: one row per ACLED country, its population and GDP per capita for 2020 to 2023 and their means as columns; a lookup table for merging, no model.

One row per cell of ship type, construction period and operation period, with accidents and months of service (McCullagh and Nelder 1983; Greene 2003, Table F21.3), the three classifying factors fitted as fixed effects with a log service offset; no cluster column.
One row per Californian metropolitan area in 1972 (Verbeek 2004, ch. 4); no cluster column.
One row per takeover target firm (docno), the number of bids a count regression response (Cameron and Trivedi 1998, ch. 5); no cluster column.
One row per Spanish household in 1980 (Delgado and Mora 1998); town is a five-class town size, not a cluster.
One row per British household 1980-1982 with six budget shares (Blundell, Duncan and Pendakur 1998); no cluster column.
One row per Belgian worker in 1994 (Verbeek 2004, ch. 3); no cluster column.
One row per worker of the Current Population Survey in two survey years (Stock and Watson 2003, ch. 3); no cluster column.
Counts of CRAN packages at dates (Fox 2009), one series.
Daily returns 1989-1998 of three stocks and the CRSP index as columns, one series each (Davidson and MacKinnon 2004).
One row per respondent's stated choice among six vehicles, the alternatives' attributes as columns (McFadden and Train 2000); one choice per respondent, no cluster column.
One row per Dutch men's fashion store in 1990 (Verbeek 2004, ch. 3); no cluster column.

One row per price listing of a 486 PC, 1993-1995 (Stengos and Zacharias 2005); trend counts months and enters the hedonic price model as a time trend, and no maker or model column groups the listings.
Quarterly Canadian disposable income and consumption 1947-1996, one series (Davidson and MacKinnon 2004).
One row per diamond (Chu 2001); colour, clarity and certification body classify the stones, no cluster column.
One row per person in 1986, doctor visits a count response (Gurmu 1997; Davidson and MacKinnon 2004, ch. 11); no cluster column.
One row per respondent of the 1977-1978 Australian Health Survey (Cameron and Trivedi 1986; 1998, ch. 3); no cluster column.

RAND Health Insurance Experiment person-years (Deb and Trivedi 2002): individuals recur over years and within families, as the repeated family variables show, but the table has no person or family identifier.
One row per earner in three age groups (Mills and Zandvakili 1997); age is a three-level class, no cluster column.
One row per respondent of the extramarital affairs survey (Fair 1977; Greene 2003, Table F22.2); no cluster column.
One row per angler's fishing mode choice, the four modes' prices and catch rates as columns (Herriges and Kling 1999); one choice per angler, no cluster column.
One row per game show contestant with the partner's attributes and choice as columns (Kalist 2004); no pair or episode column, and season and round have two and three levels.
Daily exchange rates of the US dollar against five currencies 1980-1987 as columns, one series each (Verbeek 2004, ch. 8).

wide: one row per young man, two waves (the first observation and 1980) of southern residence, marriage, SMSA, age, schooling, experience, tenure and log wage as paired columns (Blackburn and Neumark 1992; Hayashi 2000, ch. 3).
One row per household's heating and cooling system choice, the seven systems' installation and operating costs as columns (Train); one choice per household, no cluster column.
One row per wife in 1993 with a sampling weight (Olson 1998); region has four levels, no cluster column.
The Boston HMDA table under the name it had up to Ecdat 0.2-9, a copy of Hmda with the column spelled comdominiom; the page is Hmda's.
One row per household (idcase) choosing among five heating systems, their costs as columns (Train); region has four levels, no cluster column.
One row per Boston mortgage applicant (Munnell et al. 1996), the binary deny modeled by probit and logit in Stock and Watson (2003, ch. 9); no cluster column.
One row per house sold in Windsor in 1987 (Anglin and Gencay 1996); no neighborhood column beside the binary prefarea.
Four-weekly ice cream consumption, income, price and temperature 1951-1953, one series (Hildreth and Lu 1960; Verbeek 2004, ch. 4).
One row per respondent of the double-bounded contingent valuation survey on Kakadu National Park; no cluster column.
One row per Belgian firm in 1996 (Verbeek 2004, ch. 4); no cluster column.
One row per Massachusetts school district in 1997-1998 (Stock and Watson 2003, ch. 7); municipality and district name the row, no cluster column.
One row per student of intermediate economics (Butler, Finegan and Siegfried 1998); no cluster column.
RAND Health Insurance Experiment individuals (Deb and Trivedi 2002): members of one family recur, as the repeated family variables show, but the table has no person or family identifier.
One row per traveler's mode choice, the four modes' cost and time as columns (Train); one choice per traveler, no cluster column.
Long choice table of Greene (2003, Table F21.2): each traveler takes four rows (air, train, bus, car) with mode the 0/1 chosen indicator, but the table holds no traveler or alternative column.
One row per host country of US majority-owned foreign affiliates in 1982 (Ioannatos 1995); no cluster column.
One row per married woman in 1975 (Mroz labor supply data); the county unemployment rate has no county identifier beside it.
One row per respondent of the double-bounded contingent valuation survey on the Alentejo Natural Park (Nunes 2000; Verbeek 2004, ch. 7); no cluster column.
One row per US electricity producer in 1955 (Nerlove 1963; Greene 2003, Table F14.2); no cluster column.
One row per elderly person of the National Medical Expenditure Survey (Deb and Trivedi 1997); region has three levels, no cluster column.
One row per UK North Sea oil field, a duration model of the appraisal lag (Favero, Pesaran and Sharma 1994); no cluster column.
Monthly frozen orange juice price, finished goods price index and freezing degree days 1948-2001, one series (Stock and Watson 2003).
One row per Swiss woman, labor force participation a binary response (Gerfin 1996; Davidson and MacKinnon 2004, ch. 11); no cluster column.
